steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Draft the introduction for our paper on light continual training of already-trained LLMs by reweighting hard samples from the original training data. Motivate it with concerns about running out of high-quality data, describe our loss-based sample selection observation and the IR-DRO method, and end with a contribution list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLM abilities and the scale of pretraining data
2. Data shortage concern and the research question
3. Observation on high-loss samples and an empirical selection strategy
4. IR-DRO as a principled alternative
5. Experiments and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs and data
- impressive understanding/reasoning in multiple tasks; surprising abilities such as in-context learning
- trained on extensive corpora: web-crawled documents, scholarly articles
- LLaMA pretraining: up to one trillion word tokens; GPT-4 reportedly more than 13 trillion tokens

2. Concern + question
- increasing token counts a concern; depletion of high-quality data sources; projected shortfall by 2026
- synthetic data helps in some downstream tasks, but domain shifts and biases -> "real" high-quality data still preferred
- recent studies: carefully selected high-quality data is critical for LLM performance
- question: given a trained LLM, improve via light continual training by exploiting samples from same training dataset?
- benefit: conserve compute already invested, better performance without additional data

3. Empirical strategy
- examine samples with high and small loss values (Section 3.2)
- traditional strategy of always selecting highest-loss samples can impair LLM performance after continual training
- manual examination: such samples more likely noise or inherently challenging patterns (online advertisements, reference lists from papers)
- proposal: select samples with moderately high loss
- proof-of-concept: continual pretraining with this strategy improves performance on various benchmarks

4. IR-DRO
- empirical strategy needs trial and error for hyperparameters, model-specific
- Instance-Reweighted Distributionally Robust Optimization (IR-DRO): automatically identify and prioritize informative samples, no tedious tuning
- closed-form formulation -> easy integration into existing LLM training pipelines

5. Experiments + contributions
- IR-DRO outperforms empirical strategy on various benchmarks
- versatile: also improves other scenarios incl. instruction tuning
- contributions: empirical algorithm selecting moderate-complexity instances (based on textual patterns); IR-DRO, instance reweighting, dynamic prioritization; experiments on OPT, Sheared-LLaMA, LLaMA -> improvements after continual pre-training and instruction tuning

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to understand and reason in multiple tasks, and they also have some surprising abilities like in-context learning. To train these models we need an extensive corpus of data, which includes web-crawled documents and scholarly articles. For example, pretraining a LLaMA model uses up to one trillion word tokens, and GPT-4 reportedly uses more than 13 trillion tokens for pretraining.

But the increasing number of tokens used for pretraining LLMs has become a concern. It has been suggested that running out of high-quality data sources may become a more and more pressing challenge, and projections show there may be a shortfall in the supply of such data by 2026. High-quality synthetic data can help with the shortage of data in some downstream tasks, but it is recognized that synthetic data often has domain shifts and biases, so high-quality "real" training data is still preferred for training LLMs. Recent studies have also stressed that carefully selected, high-quality data plays a critical role in improving LLM performance. Because of these observations we ask a research question: if we already have a trained LLM, how can we further improve its performance with light continual training, by strategically using the samples from the same training dataset? Answering this can save the computational effort that was already put into LLMs and improve performance without more data.

To answer this question about continual training of LLMs, we start by looking at the samples that have high and small loss values. Our results, which we detail in Section 3.2, show a noteworthy observation: the traditional strategy of always selecting the samples with the highest losses can hurt LLM performance after continuous training. When we examine examples manually, we see that these samples are more likely to be associated with noise or with patterns that are inherently challenging, for example online advertisements and reference lists from papers. To deal with this, we propose an empirical strategy that selects samples with a moderately high level of loss. Our proof-of-concept experiments show that using this strategy for continual pretraining improves performance on various evaluation benchmark datasets.

IR-DRO
- empirical strategy: hyperparameters need trial and error, model-specific
- Instance-Reweighted Distributionally Robust Optimization (IR-DRO): automatically identify/prioritize informative samples, no tedious tuning
- closed-form formulation -> easy integration into existing LLM training pipelines

Experiments and contributions
- IR-DRO beats empirical strategy on various benchmarks; also helps instruction tuning
- contribution 1: empirical algorithm picking moderate-complexity instances, based on textual patterns
- contribution 2: IR-DRO, instance reweighting, dynamic prioritization of informative samples
- contribution 3: experiments on OPT, Sheared-LLaMA, LLaMA; gains after continual pre-training and instruction tuning

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to understand and reason in multiple tasks, and they also have some surprising abilities like in-context learning. To train these models we need an extensive corpus of data, which includes web-crawled documents and scholarly articles. For example, pretraining a LLaMA model uses up to one trillion word tokens, and GPT-4 reportedly uses more than 13 trillion tokens for pretraining.

But the increasing number of tokens used for pretraining LLMs has become a concern. It has been suggested that running out of high-quality data sources may become a more and more pressing challenge, and projections show there may be a shortfall in the supply of such data by 2026. High-quality synthetic data can help with the shortage of data in some downstream tasks, but it is recognized that synthetic data often has domain shifts and biases, so high-quality "real" training data is still preferred for training LLMs. Recent studies have also stressed that carefully selected, high-quality data plays a critical role in improving LLM performance. Because of these observations we ask a research question: if we already have a trained LLM, how can we further improve its performance with light continual training, by strategically using the samples from the same training dataset? Answering this can save the computational effort that was already put into LLMs and improve performance without more data.

To answer this question about continual training of LLMs, we start by looking at the samples that have high and small loss values. Our results, which we detail in Section 3.2, show a noteworthy observation: the traditional strategy of always selecting the samples with the highest losses can hurt LLM performance after continuous training. When we examine examples manually, we see that these samples are more likely to be associated with noise or with patterns that are inherently challenging, for example online advertisements and reference lists from papers. To deal with this, we propose an empirical strategy that selects samples with a moderately high level of loss. Our proof-of-concept experiments show that using this strategy for continual pretraining improves performance on various evaluation benchmark datasets.

This empirical strategy is effective, but choosing the right hyperparameters needs trial and error and has to be done for each model. So we present a more principled algorithm, called Instance-Reweighted Distributionally Robust Optimization (IR-DRO), which automatically identifies and prioritizes informative samples that are beneficial to continual training, without a tedious hyperparameter tuning process. We have also developed a closed-form formulation so that IR-DRO can be easily integrated into existing training pipelines of LLMs.

Our experiments show that IR-DRO does better than our empirical strategy on various benchmarks. We also show that our techniques are versatile and can improve other training scenarios, including instruction tuning. Our contributions are:

- To identify samples that are beneficial for continual training of LLMs, we introduce an empirical algorithm that selects instances with moderate levels of complexity. This approach is based on what we observed about textual patterns, and it is effective in improving the performance of continually trained models.

- We also adapt and develop IR-DRO, a principled algorithm based on optimization that uses the instance reweighting formulation to dynamically identify and prioritize crucial and informative samples for continual training of LLMs.

- We do extensive experiments on various pre-trained models, such as OPT, Sheared-LLaMA, and LLaMA, and they confirm that our algorithms are effective. Our methods get improved performance on evaluation benchmarks after continual pre-training and after instruction tuning.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated an impressive ability to understand and reason in multiple tasks and have shown surprising abilities such as in-context learning [1,2]. These models require training on an extensive corpus of data, including web-crawled documents [3] and scholarly articles [4]. For example, the pretraining of a LLaMA model consumes up to one trillion word tokens, and GPT-4 [5] reportedly uses more than 13 trillion tokens for pretraining.

However, the increasing number of tokens used for pretraining LLMs has become a concern. It has been suggested that the depletion of high-quality data sources may become an increasingly pressing challenge, with projections indicating a potential shortfall in the supply of such data by 2026 [6]. While high-quality synthetic data can help mitigate the data shortage in some downstream tasks [7,8], it is recognized that such data often has domain shifts [9] and biases [10], so high-quality "real" training data is still preferred for LLM training. Recent studies [11,12,13] have also emphasized the critical role of carefully selected, high-quality data in enhancing LLM performance. These observations raise a research question: Given an already trained LLM, how can we further improve its performance through light continual training, by strategically exploiting samples from the same training dataset? Addressing this can conserve the computational effort already invested in LLMs and increase performance without additional data.

To answer this question regarding the continual training of LLMs, we begin by examining the samples associated with high and small loss values. Our results, detailed in Section 3.2, reveal a noteworthy observation: the traditional strategy of always selecting samples with the highest losses can impair LLM performance after continuous training. Manual examination of examples shows that these samples are more likely to be associated with noise or inherently challenging patterns, such as those found in online advertisements and reference lists from papers. To address this issue, we propose an empirical strategy that selects samples exhibiting a moderately high level of loss. Our proof-of-concept experiments demonstrate that applying this strategy to continual pretraining enhances performance on various evaluation benchmark datasets.

Despite its effectiveness, this empirical strategy requires trial and error to choose proper hyperparameters for each model. In response, we present a more principled algorithm, called Instance-Reweighted Distributionally Robust Optimization (IR-DRO), which automatically identifies and prioritizes informative samples that benefit continual training, without a tedious hyperparameter tuning process. We have also developed a closed-form formulation that allows IR-DRO to be integrated straightforwardly into existing LLM training pipelines.

Our experiments demonstrate that IR-DRO outperforms our empirical strategy on various benchmarks. We further show that our proposed techniques are versatile and can improve other training scenarios, including instruction tuning. Our contributions are summarized below:

- To identify samples beneficial for the continual training of LLMs, we introduce an empirical algorithm that selects instances with moderate complexity levels. This approach is based on our observations of textual patterns and proves effective in enhancing the performance of continually trained models.

- We further adapt and develop IR-DRO, a principled optimization-based algorithm that uses the instance reweighting formulation to dynamically identify and prioritize crucial and informative samples for the continual training of LLMs.

- Extensive experiments on various pre-trained models, such as OPT [14], Sheared-LLaMA [15], and LLaMA [16], confirm the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms. Our methods improve performance on evaluation benchmarks after continual pre-training and instruction tuning, respectively.
